01 · revision, then the turn

From "what groups exist" to "what doesn't belong"

Quick reminder of where this module has been: every input is unlabeled — no target column, ever. Classes 01–06 spent their entire time on ONE question asked of that unlabeled data: group it. K-Means, K-Means++, Hierarchical Clustering, GMM, DBSCAN — five different algorithms, five different mechanisms, all in service of the same goal: find the natural groups.

ClassAlgorithmQuestion it answered
01–02K-Means, K-Means++What K centroid-based groups explain this data?
03Hierarchical ClusteringWhat nested groups exist at every scale at once?
04GMMWhat overlapping, probabilistic groups (soft membership) exist?
05–06DBSCANWhat DENSITY-based groups exist, with noise as a side-effect?

Today, same unlabeled input — but the question flips entirely. We stop asking "what groups exist" and start asking something narrower and, in a lot of real businesses, far more urgent:

"We spent several classes learning how to find groups. What if I don't actually care about the groups? What if I care about the observations that behave strangely?"
The one definition to hold onto for this entire class: most observations follow some expected pattern. An anomaly is an observation that significantly deviates from that expected pattern. The hard part — the part every method below handles differently — is that "expected" is always relative to a population, never an absolute property of a single number.

Clustering asks

"What groups exist?"

vs

Anomaly detection asks

"Which observations do not behave like the expected population?"

02 · why this matters, before the math

What is an anomaly, and why industries pay real money to catch one

Same underlying question — "does this observation fit the population it's supposed to belong to" — shows up under wildly different names across industries. Recognizing the pattern is half the skill.

DomainNormal patternThe anomalyThe question actually asked
Banking / fraudMost transactions ₹500–₹10,000, familiar locations₹4,50,000 transaction at 3AM from another country"Does this deserve investigation?"
ManufacturingStable vibration & temperature readingsA machine's readings suddenly spike together"Is this machine behaving abnormally?"
Network securityTypical login times, locations, data volumes per userLogin from a new country, odd hour, huge data transfer"Is this account compromised?"
Healthcare monitoringVitals within the typical range for this patient's profileA sudden, sharp deviation in one or more vitals"Does this patient need immediate attention?"
E-commerceTypical order size and frequency per accountA first-time account places a bulk order 3× the usual size"Reseller, bot, or fraud ring?"

Take the banking row apart for a second, because the exact numbers matter for intuition. Most of this customer's transactions sit somewhere around ₹500 to ₹10,000 — call the "normal-looking" range roughly ₹1,000–₹25,000 once you allow for a few bigger, still-ordinary purchases. A transaction of ₹4,50,000 at 3AM from a country this card has never been used in sits nowhere near that range on ANY dimension — amount, time, location — stacked together.

Flagged is not the same as guilty. A flagged transaction means "investigate" — not "block" and not "confirmed fraud." A single huge, legitimate purchase (a wedding, a laptop, an emergency flight) will also get flagged by every method in this class. The anomaly detector's job stops at "this doesn't look like the expected pattern" — a human, a rule engine, or a follow-up verification step decides what to do next.

Why not just train a classifier on "is this fraud"?

This is the question every new student asks, and it has a real answer, not just a hand-wave. Confirmed fraud labels are rare (a tiny fraction of a percent of transactions), expensive to obtain (someone has to investigate and confirm), and structurally biased (you only ever get labels for fraud patterns your OLD detection system already caught — genuinely novel fraud tricks are, by definition, underrepresented or absent from your training labels). A supervised classifier trained on that label set learns "yesterday's fraud," not "fraud." Anomaly detection sidesteps the entire problem: it learns what NORMAL looks like from the abundant, cheap, unlabeled data you already have, and flags departures from it — including fraud patterns nobody has ever seen or labeled before.

03 · vocabulary, precisely

Outlier, novelty, anomaly — same idea, three different contexts

These three words get used interchangeably in casual conversation, and for most of this class that's fine. But scikit-learn draws a real, functional line between them — worth knowing precisely, once, so you never have to guess again.

TermDefinitionWhat the training data looks likeWhere it's detected
OutlierA point already IN your dataset that looks different from the restMay already contain some outliers — that's exactly what you're hunting forWithin the SAME dataset you fit on
NoveltyA point unlike anything the model has seen beforeAssumed entirely clean — no outliers present during trainingNEW, unseen data at prediction time
AnomalyThe umbrella term for either—Used loosely; context decides which of the two you mean
A preview, not lecture content — we'll use this hands-on next session. In scikit-learn, this exact distinction shows up as a literal constructor argument on LocalOutlierFactor: novelty=False means "find outliers within the data I'm fitting on, right now"; novelty=True means "assume my training data is clean — now judge brand-new points against it." The underlying math (everything in Section 08) is identical either way — only what you're allowed to call .predict() on afterward changes. Nothing to memorize today; it'll make more sense once you've written the code.
04 · four tools, one job

Four ways to ask "does this point belong?"

Every method below answers the exact same underlying question, but each one asks it in a completely different vocabulary — statistical, geometric, structural, or density-based. Knowing WHICH question a method is asking is the fastest way to predict when it will fail.

MethodThe question it asks
IQRIs this feature unusually high or low, on its own?
Elliptic EnvelopeDoes this point fit the assumed multivariate Gaussian population?
Isolation ForestHow easily can this point be isolated from everyone else?
LOFIs this point substantially less dense than its own neighbors?
SituationReasonable starting point
One numeric variableIQR
Gaussian-like multivariate dataElliptic Envelope
Large, nonlinear tabular dataIsolation Forest
Local-density anomalies (normal globally, weird locally)LOF

The rest of this class builds each one from first principles, in exactly this order — each method's own weakness is precisely what motivates the next one.

05 · the first, simplest tool

IQR — flag what's unusual on ONE feature at a time

Already familiar from the probability distributions lecture — this is the exact same box-plot machinery, now pointed at a new job: flagging individual values as statistical outliers.

definitions $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$     $\text{Lower fence} = Q_1 - 1.5\times\text{IQR}$     $\text{Upper fence} = Q_3 + 1.5\times\text{IQR}$

$Q_1$ = 25th percentile, $Q_3$ = 75th percentile — a robust description of the middle 50% of the data, chosen precisely because a few huge values can't drag the median or the quartiles around the way they'd drag a mean and standard deviation. Any value landing outside the fences is flagged as a statistical outlier.

Step-by-step, on real numbers

1
Take the data: 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 22, 80. Find $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ using your chosen percentile convention.
2
Compute IQR $= Q_3 - Q_1$.
3
Expand the middle range by $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ on each side to get the fences.
4
Any value outside the fences is flagged as a statistical outlier.
5
Then ask the business question: is that outlier actually meaningful? IQR cannot answer this part — it only finds candidates.
$Q_1=13.25$, $Q_3=19.5$, IQR$=6.25$ → fences at $[3.875,\ 28.875]$. Only 80 falls outside — everything else, including 22, is well within bounds.
Critical distinction: IQR flags statistical outliers according to a univariate fence. It does not know whether the observation is fraudulent, broken, malicious, or clinically dangerous — that judgment is a separate, downstream step, human or otherwise.

The blind spot: IQR checks each feature completely alone

This technique is applied to individual features, not to whole observations. So the obvious next question: what if the decision depends on the RELATIONSHIP between two features, not either one alone?

A real correlated 2D dataset. The starred point passes BOTH per-feature fences individually — IQR sees nothing wrong on either axis — yet it sits at Mahalanobis distance ≈4.1 from the joint pattern, versus ≈1.2 average for genuinely normal points. IQR is structurally blind to this entire category of anomaly.
IQR doesn't capture the relationship between features. Two per-feature-normal values combined can still be a completely abnormal COMBINATION — a transaction amount that's fine on its own, at a distance-from-home that's fine on its own, but a combination ("large amount, far from home") that essentially never occurs together in this customer's real history. IQR, checking one axis at a time, cannot see this. That gap is exactly what Elliptic Envelope exists to close.
06 · when the RELATIONSHIP between features matters

Elliptic Envelope — fit one Gaussian "shape," flag what falls outside it

Elliptic Envelope follows a strong, explicit assumption: your data comes from a single, unimodal, multivariate Gaussian distribution. If we draw the corresponding ellipse (2D) or ellipsoid (higher-D) around that distribution, anything that lands outside it is treated as an outlier.

How is this different from GMM? GMM (Class 04) fits MULTIPLE Gaussian components — each cluster gets its own little ellipse, which is exactly how GMM handled multi-modal data. Elliptic Envelope deliberately fits only ONE Gaussian across the entire dataset. That's not a missing feature — it's the whole design. GMM's job is finding several groups; Elliptic Envelope's job is testing a single "this is one population" hypothesis and flagging violations of it. One ellipse, one distribution — never multiple, by construction.

How it works, step by step

1
Estimate the center ($\mu$) and covariance ($\Sigma$) of the presumed normal population.
2
Use a robust covariance estimator so a few contaminated observations don't drag the fit around — scikit-learn's implementation uses Fast-MCD (Fast Minimum Covariance Determinant), a linear-algebra technique for this exact purpose. You don't need the internals of Fast-MCD to use this algorithm well; just know it exists specifically so outliers can't corrupt their own detector.
3
Define an elliptical / ellipsoidal region around the fitted population.
4
Use a distance score relative to that fitted shape — this is the Mahalanobis distance, covered just below.
5
Use the threshold implied by the contamination setting to decide which observations get flagged.
Real EllipticEnvelope fit, contamination=5%, on the exact same data as the IQR figure above. The phantom point IQR missed entirely is now correctly outside the ellipse (decision score −17.9). μ marks the fitted center; the ellipse's tilt IS the fitted covariance.

μ and Σ — what you actually get out of the fit

$\mu$ is simply the fitted mean vector — the ellipse's center. $\Sigma$, the covariance matrix, captures both each feature's individual spread AND how the features move together (their correlation) — it's precisely this second part, absent from IQR entirely, that lets the ellipse tilt to match the real diagonal relationship in the data instead of sitting as an axis-aligned box.

Optional — Mahalanobis distance: why not just use Euclidean distance from μ?
Mahalanobis distance$D_M(x) = \sqrt{(x-\mu)^{\top}\, \Sigma^{-1} \,(x-\mu)}$

Euclidean distance treats every direction from $\mu$ as equally "far." Mahalanobis distance stretches that notion of distance using $\Sigma^{-1}$ — a direction the data naturally varies a lot ALONG gets treated as "closer than it looks," and a direction the data almost never varies ACROSS gets treated as "farther than it looks." It's distance measured in units of "how surprising is this, given how this data actually spreads."

Points A and B are the exact same Euclidean distance from μ (34.4 both). Mahalanobis says A=2.4σ (it moved WITH the natural correlation — unsurprising) and B=8.4σ (it moved AGAINST the correlation — genuinely rare). Same raw distance, very different meaning.

How outliers get detected from this: compute $D_M(x)$ for every point, then flag whichever points sit at the extreme end — the exact cutoff is set by the contamination parameter, described next.

The contamination factor

Contamination is a number you set — say 0.1 — meaning "I expect roughly 10% of this population to be outliers." Two things happen with this number, not just one: it sets the final flagging threshold (points scoring worst by Mahalanobis distance, up to that fraction, get flagged), AND it feeds directly into the robust Fast-MCD fit itself (step 2 above) — telling the covariance estimator how many of the worst-looking points it's allowed to down-weight while estimating $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ in the first place, so the ellipse isn't corrupted by the very outliers it's trying to find.

Optional — does "multiple Elliptic Envelope" exist?

Checked directly: scikit-learn's EllipticEnvelope only ever supports ONE Gaussian per fit — there is no built-in "multiple ellipse" variant in scikit-learn. You could, in principle, cluster the data first (K-Means or GMM) and fit a separate EllipticEnvelope per cluster, approximating a multi-ellipse detector — but that's a manual composition of two algorithms, not a single named, off-the-shelf method. Worth knowing it's conceptually possible; not worth treating as a standard tool.

Disadvantages — where it visibly breaks

  • Cannot be used on non-unimodal data. The whole method is built around fitting exactly one Gaussian.
  • Specifically assumes multivariate Gaussian structure. If the data fails unimodal + multivariate-Gaussian, the whole thing crashes conceptually — not literally an error, but a meaningless fit.
  • May break, or underperform badly, in high-dimensional settings. As a rule of thumb, take care to work with $n_{\text{samples}} \gg n_{\text{features}}^2$.
Failure mode 1: two real, separate, legitimate clusters. One ellipse spans both — the empty gap between them scores as a confident inlier (score +7.3), because one ellipse literally cannot distinguish "inside the shape" from "inside either actual cluster."
Failure mode 2: a curved manifold. An ellipse can only ever be convex, so it necessarily covers the empty space "inside" the curve's bend — the marked point scores as a confident inlier (score +29.2) despite sitting nowhere near the real data.
07 · tree-based, no distance, no distribution assumption

Isolation Forest — anomalies are "few and different," so isolate them

A complete change of strategy. Instead of asking "what does normal look like" (Elliptic Envelope's question), Isolation Forest asks: how quickly can I separate this point from everyone else?

Imagine a person standing alone in an empty stadium. You need very little effort to isolate them. A person inside a dense crowd is much harder to isolate.— the entire intuition behind Isolation Forest, in one image

Why "forest," why tree-based

Isolation Forests (IF) are built on decision trees, similar to Random Forests — but since there are no labels anywhere in this problem, it's an unsupervised model; hence also called an iForest. And this is the detail every student trips on first: there is no information gain, no entropy, no target to optimize a split against — because there is no label. So what decides each split?

The split rule, stated exactly: randomly pick a feature. Randomly choose a threshold, uniformly between that feature's current min and max. Partition the data into "below" and "at-or-above." That's it — no criterion is being maximized. The split is random, on purpose.

The algorithm, step by step

1
Randomly select a feature. For a transaction, this could be amount, hour, distance-from-home — any column, chosen uniformly at random.
2
Randomly choose a split threshold between that feature's minimum and maximum value, within the current subset of points.
3
Partition the data into values below the threshold and values at-or-above it.
4
Recurse inside the partition containing the point of interest.
5
Continue until the point is isolated alone in its own leaf, or the tree reaches its height limit.
6
The number of splits traversed to reach that leaf is the point's path length.
Real from-scratch isolation tree, same random-split rule applied to both points. The outlier's own box shrinks to contain only itself after just 1 split; the ordinary, centrally-located inlier takes 6 splits to isolate the exact same way.
The whole idea, summarized: on average, outliers have LOWER depth in the random trees — they sit in empty, sparse regions that a random cut is likely to slice off almost immediately. On average, inliers have MORE depth — a random cut is unlikely to separate them from their many close neighbors in just one or two tries; it takes many nested cuts to peel a typical point away from a dense crowd.

Multiple trees → the forest, and how depth becomes a score

A single random tree is noisy — one unlucky sequence of random splits could isolate an ordinary point quickly by chance. So Isolation Forest builds MANY such trees (typically on a random subsample of the data per tree, not the full dataset), computes each point's path length in EVERY tree, and averages across the whole forest. That average, not any single tree's result, is the stable signal.

Real forest of 100 trees (subsample size 32), on the same phantom-point dataset from Sections 05–06. Left: raw average path length — 3 typical points average 6.6–7.4 splits; the phantom outlier averages just 4.4. Right: the same numbers converted to the standard iForest anomaly score.
Internal details (optional) — the exact scoring formula
isolation forest anomaly score$s(x,n) = 2^{-\frac{E(h(x))}{c(n)}}$

$E(h(x))$ is the average path length for point $x$ across all trees (the bar chart above, left panel). $c(n)$ is a normalization constant — the average path length of an unsuccessful search in a binary search tree of $n$ points, $c(n) = 2(\ln(n-1)+\gamma) - \frac{2(n-1)}{n}$ where $\gamma \approx 0.5772$ (Euler–Mascheroni constant). This normalization is what keeps scores comparable regardless of subsample size, and lands them in a predictable range: scores near 1 = strongly anomalous, near 0.5 = no strong signal either way, well below 0.5 = strongly normal.

Cross-checked against real sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest on the identical points: our from-scratch scores (0.432, 0.474, 0.452, 0.603) matched sklearn's own (0.435, 0.464, 0.452, 0.583) closely — same ranking, same conclusion, small differences only from each forest's own independent random trees.

Exactly like the other methods, the contamination setting turns this continuous score into a binary flag — the worst-scoring fraction of points, matching the contamination rate, get flagged as outliers.

Major disadvantage — bias toward axis-parallel splits

Every single split Isolation Forest ever makes is parallel to one of the axes — that's a direct consequence of "pick ONE feature, threshold it." The decision boundary this produces is therefore always axis-aligned, never smoothly curved or diagonal, no matter how much data you throw at it.

Real IsolationForest score heatmap on an isotropic (perfectly circular) blob. P1 and P2 sit at the IDENTICAL Euclidean distance from the center — one on-axis, one diagonal — yet score differently (−0.604 vs −0.659). The cross-shaped score field is the axis-parallel bias made visible.
08 · when even Isolation Forest isn't local enough

Local Outlier Factor — "unusual compared to WHOM?"

Isolation Forest asks a GLOBAL question: how easily can this point be isolated from the WHOLE population? LOF asks something narrower and sharper.

A point can be globally ordinary but locally strange. So compare it to its neighbors.— the entire idea behind LOF

The core idea rests on two familiar ingredients: KNN and density. Compare the density around a point to the density around its $k$ nearest neighbors. If the point's own neighborhood is meaningfully less dense than its neighbors' neighborhoods, flag it. This is exactly the situation Isolation Forest can miss — a point sitting in a legitimately sparser pocket right next to a very dense cluster, without being extreme on any GLOBAL scale.

Building LOF from first principles, in five steps: distance → k-nearest-neighbors → k-distance → reachability distance → local reachability density → LOF. Each step is one small, concrete idea — nothing here needs anything beyond what you already know.

Step 1 — k-distance and $N_k(A)$

k-distance(A) is the distance from point $A$ to its $k$-th nearest neighbor. For a chosen $k$ (say $k{=}3$): how far do I have to go before I encounter my 3rd nearest neighbor? A SHORT k-distance means $A$ sits in a dense neighborhood; a LONG k-distance means $A$ sits somewhere sparse. $N_k(A)$ is simply the set of those $k$ nearest neighbors.

Real worked example, $k{=}3$: k-distance(C1) = 0.583 — the radius that first reaches C1's 3rd-nearest neighbor. $N_3(\text{C1}) = \{\text{C4, C3, C5}\}$.

Step 2 — reachability distance

reachability distance$\text{reach-dist}(a,b) = \max\big(\text{k-distance}(b),\ d(a,b)\big)$

From point $a$ to point $b$: take whichever is LARGER — the real distance between them, or $b$'s OWN k-distance. Why use $b$'s k-distance at all? It's a smoothing factor: if $a$ is already well within $b$'s own dense neighborhood, treat the "effective" distance as $b$'s local scale, not the tiny raw distance, which would otherwise make $b$ look artificially even denser than it is.

Two real cases from the same dataset. Left: the real distance dominates (C4's own neighborhood is tighter than its distance to C1). Right: the neighbor's own k-distance dominates (C3's neighborhood floor is larger than the raw gap to Plocal) — Plocal doesn't get credit for landing "suspiciously close" to a point whose whole neighborhood is spread that wide anyway.

Step 3 — Local Reachability Density (LRD)

local reachability density$\text{LRD}_k(a) = \dfrac{k}{\sum_{o \in N_k(a)} \text{reach-dist}(a,o)}$

Average the reachability distances to all $k$ neighbors, then take the reciprocal. Intuitively: LRD tells you how far you typically have to travel from $a$ to reach its neighbors. Short average reach-distance → high density → HIGH LRD. Long average reach-distance → sparse → LOW LRD.

Same formula, two real neighborhoods. C1 (dense cluster member): LRD ≈ 1.14. Pglobal (the far outlier): LRD ≈ 0.13 — nearly 9× lower, purely because its reach-distances are so much larger.

Step 4 — LOF itself

local outlier factor$\text{LOF}_k(a) = \dfrac{1}{k}\displaystyle\sum_{o \in N_k(a)} \dfrac{\text{LRD}_k(o)}{\text{LRD}_k(a)} \;=\; \dfrac{\text{avg}\big(\text{LRD of }a\text{'s neighbors}\big)}{\text{LRD}(a)}$

LOF is the average ratio of $a$'s neighbors' LRDs to $a$'s own LRD. If that ratio is greater than 1, $a$'s neighborhood is on average LESS dense than its neighbors' own neighborhoods — meaning $a$ has to travel farther to reach its cluster than its neighbors do to reach theirs.

See it computed, one point at a time

Let's calculate LOF for three different points on the exact same small dataset, one at a time, so you can see precisely how the number changes with what's actually around each point. Every number below is computed from scratch and cross-checked against real sklearn.neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor — exact match to 4 decimal places.

C1 (deep inside the dense cluster) → LOF ≈ 1.21. Plocal (near the cluster's edge, locally sparse) → LOF ≈ 2.76. Pglobal (the far, obvious outlier) → LOF ≈ 9.86. Same five steps, run three times, on the same 8-point dataset, $k{=}3$ throughout.
PointLRD(point)avg neighbor LRDLOFReading

C41.4141.2700.900Slightly DENSER than its own neighbors
Plocal0.5111.4112.758A real LOCAL outlier — not globally extreme, but locally sparse

C2C6, C4, C10.632C6: max(0.632,0.566)=0.632  ·  C4: max(0.906,0.632)=0.906  ·  C1: max(0.583,0.632)=0.6323/2.170 = 1.382
C1C4, C3, C50.583C4: max(0.906,0.566)=0.906  ·  C3: max(0.825,0.583)=0.825  ·  C5: max(0.906,0.583)=0.9063/2.636 = 1.138

Step 3 — put it together. avg neighbor LRD = (1.414 + 1.382 + 1.138) / 3 = 1.312. LOF(Pglobal) = 1.312 / 0.133 = 9.861 — its own neighborhood is nearly 10× less dense than its neighbors'. No ambiguity here, locally or globally.

Interpreting the LOF value

LOF valueMeaning
≈ 1Same density as its neighbors → normal
> 1 (mildly)Neighbors are somewhat denser — not conclusive on its own; could go either way
≫ 1Neighbors are MUCH denser → a genuine, strong local outlier
< 1Point is DENSER than its own neighbors → if anything, extra "normal," core-like

A worked reference from the table above: extreme outliers get very high LOF; border points of a dense region get only slightly-above-1 values, and we don't mark those as outliers. Plocal's 2.76 is a genuinely elevated, real local anomaly; Pglobal's 9.86 needs no further debate.

When LOF fails, and how to choose k

  • Finding the optimal k — there is no formula; too small a $k$ makes LOF noisy and overly sensitive to one nearby point, too large a $k$ averages over too broad a neighborhood and starts washing out genuinely local anomalies, behaving more like a global method instead. Practically: sweep a handful of candidate $k$ values (the exact same stability-range instinct from Class 06 §05's MinPts search) and look for a range where results stay consistent, rather than searching for one "correct" number.
  • Finding the threshold — LOF(A) ≫ 1 sounds clear until you have to write code: what exact cutoff counts as "≫"? In practice this is set via the contamination parameter (Section 09), not a fixed universal number.
  • Cannot handle high-dimensional data efficiently — like every distance-based method, LOF suffers from the curse of dimensionality: in high dimensions, distances between points stop being meaningfully different from each other.
  • High time complexity — a k-nearest-neighbor search is required for EVERY point, making LOF meaningfully more expensive than Isolation Forest at large scale.
09 · one shared knob (mostly)

Contamination — the parameter that ties three of these four methods together

Contamination is the expected FRACTION of the dataset that is anomalous. Elliptic Envelope, Isolation Forest, and LOF all convert their own continuous score into a binary flag by thresholding at roughly the top-contamination% worst-scoring points.

Contamination settingElliptic EnvelopeIsolation ForestLOFTarget count (n=195)
— (IQR, fixed rule)no contamination knob — fence is fixed by 1.5×IQR alone14 flagged (7.2%)
0.0510 (5.1%)10 (5.1%)10 (5.1%)9.75
0.1020 (10.3%)20 (10.3%)20 (10.3%)19.5
0.2039 (20.0%)39 (20.0%)39 (20.0%)39.0

Real numbers, same 195-point dataset (a dense blob plus scattered noise), all three sklearn estimators run at each setting. Each one lands within a point or two of the exact mathematical target ($n \times \text{contamination}$) — that's not a coincidence, it's precisely what "threshold at the top-contamination% by score" means, mechanically.

IQR has no contamination knob. Its fence is fixed entirely by the $1.5\times\text{IQR}$ rule — there is no dial to turn to get exactly 5%, or exactly 10%, flagged. That's a real, structural difference worth remembering when picking a method: if your business needs "flag exactly the worst 2% for review capacity reasons," IQR alone cannot deliver that; the other three can, directly.
One extra wrinkle for Elliptic Envelope specifically: contamination there does double duty — it sets the final flagging threshold, AND it tells the robust Fast-MCD fit itself how many of the worst points it's allowed to downweight while estimating $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ (Section 06). For Isolation Forest and LOF, contamination only affects the final threshold, not how the model itself is built.
10 · head-to-head, on the same data

All four methods, same datasets — where each one wins and loses

Real code, run once, on three dataset shapes: a dense blob with scattered noise, two well-separated blobs, and two curved arcs. Contamination fixed at 8% everywhere it applies.

IQR (top row) barely reacts to the second and third datasets — 2 and 1 points flagged respectively — because per-feature fences see almost nothing wrong in either shape. Elliptic Envelope, Isolation Forest, and LOF all perform comparably well on the first two datasets; watch Elliptic Envelope's row on the arcs (right column) — it flags a couple of points right at the crossing point in the MIDDLE of the arcs, the exact multimodal/curved failure mode from Section 06, showing up organically in a head-to-head test.

11 · the elephant in the room

DBSCAN already gives you a "noise" label — so why not just use that?

Fair question, and worth answering precisely rather than hand-waving past it. DBSCAN's noise points ARE, in a real sense, already an outlier detector's output. So why does an entire new class of methods exist?

  • DBSCAN's purpose is clustering; noise is a BY-PRODUCT, not something it was built to optimize. Its two parameters (ε, MinPts) get tuned so the CLUSTER shapes and counts look right — that same tuning may not be well-suited to the specific question "how much of this should count as noise."
  • DBSCAN gives no score, only a binary label. A point either is noise or it isn't — there's no ranking, no severity, no "this is a LITTLE unusual vs. WILDLY unusual" the way LOF or Isolation Forest's continuous scores give you for free.
  • No contamination knob. You cannot ask DBSCAN "give me exactly the most-anomalous 5%" the way you can with the other three methods here — noise % is whatever falls out of (ε, MinPts), indirectly.
  • DBSCAN breaks exactly where Class 06 §06 showed it breaks — varying-density data. With clusters of genuinely different densities, one global ε makes the noise label unreliable: a real anomaly can land inside what looks like a "dense enough" neighborhood, or a legitimate sparse-cluster point can get mislabeled noise. LOF's neighborhood-relative density comparison (Section 08) is specifically immune to this.
None of this makes DBSCAN's noise label useless — quite the opposite. If you're ALREADY running DBSCAN for clustering, its noise points are a genuinely free, zero-extra-modeling-cost first-pass anomaly signal. The distinction is about what's the RIGHT primary tool when anomaly detection is the actual goal, not a side-effect.

So — when should you actually use which?

  • Already clustering with DBSCAN anyway? Use its noise label as a free first-pass anomaly flag — no reason to also run a second method just for this.
  • Need a ranked severity score, not just yes/no? LOF or Isolation Forest — both give a continuous number you can sort, threshold, or feed downstream.
  • Anomaly detection is the ONLY goal — cluster structure itself doesn't matter? Go straight to Isolation Forest, LOF, or Elliptic Envelope. Running DBSCAN here means solving a harder, unneeded problem (full cluster discovery) just to get a side-effect.
  • Local, density-varying anomalies (Class 06 §06's exact failure case)? LOF handles this natively; DBSCAN with one global ε structurally cannot.
  • Gaussian-like, well-behaved multivariate data? Elliptic Envelope is simpler and faster than either DBSCAN or LOF for this specific shape.

Concrete example: a fraud team running DBSCAN to discover behavioral customer SEGMENTS gets noise points as a free first-pass flag list — a nice bonus, no extra cost. A fraud team whose ONLY job is "score every transaction 0–1 for suspicion, then rank them for review" has no reason to run DBSCAN at all — LOF or Isolation Forest delivers that directly, without ever needing to discover clusters in the first place.

12 · wrap-up

What we covered, and what's next

IQR
per-feature fences
EE
one Gaussian ellipse
iForest
random-split isolation
LOF
local density ratio

Same unlabeled data, four completely different vocabularies for the same question: does this observation fit the population it's supposed to belong to? IQR checks one feature at a time. Elliptic Envelope checks the whole joint distribution against one Gaussian shape. Isolation Forest checks how few random cuts it takes to separate a point from everyone else. LOF checks a point's density against its own immediate neighbors, not the whole population. Each one's blind spot is exactly what motivated the next.
